questions.stem_md: A printer prints 18 pages per minute. At this rate, how many minutes will it take to print 270 pages?
On a map, 2 centimeters represent 15 kilometers. Two towns are 9 centimeters apart on the map. What is the actual distance, in kilometers, between the towns?

distractor_notes.A: This added 15 to 7.5 instead of scaling.
distractor_notes.B: This set up the proportion upside down: $9 \times \frac{2}{15}$.
distractor_notes.D: This multiplied 9 by 15, forgetting that 15 km corresponds to 2 cm, not 1 cm.

questions.stem_md: A garden hose fills a 60-gallon tank in 25 minutes. A second hose alone fills the same tank in 15 minutes. If both hoses run together, how many minutes will it take to fill the tank?
questions.explanation_md:
Add the rates:

- Hose 1: $\frac{60}{25} = 2.4$ gallons per minute.
- Hose 2: $\frac{60}{15} = 4$ gallons per minute.
- Together: $6.4$ gallons per minute.

Time: $\dfrac{60}{6.4} = 9.375 = \dfrac{75}{8}$ minutes.

(9.375 is also accepted.)

questions.stem_md: The number of members in a hiking club increased from 80 to 92. By what percent did the number of members increase?
questions.explanation_md:
Percent change is the change divided by the **original** amount:

$$\frac{92 - 80}{80} = \frac{12}{80} = 0.15 = 15\%$$

distractor_notes.A: This is the change in members (12), not a percent.
distractor_notes.B: This divided by the new amount: $12/92 \approx 13\%$.
distractor_notes.D: This is $80/92$, the old amount as a percent of the new.

questions.stem_md: The price of a stock rose by 25% on Monday and fell by 20% on Tuesday. What was the overall percent change in the price from the start of Monday to the end of Tuesday?
choices: A 5% increase
No change
A 5% decrease
A 45% increase
questions.explanation_md:
Multiply the factors: $1.25 \times 0.80 = 1.00$.

The price ended exactly where it started, so there was no change.

distractor_notes.A: Percents of different bases can’t be added: $25\% - 20\% \ne$ the overall change.
distractor_notes.C: The combined factor is exactly 1, so there is no decrease.

questions.stem_md: What is the median of the data set $12,\ 7,\ 19,\ 4,\ 15,\ 10$?
questions.explanation_md:
Sort the data: $4, 7, 10, 12, 15, 19$.

With six values, the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th values: $\frac{10 + 12}{2} = 11$.

questions.stem_md: A data set consists of the values $20, 22, 23, 25, 26$. A new value of $80$ is added to the data set. Which statement about the mean and median is true?
choices: The mean and the median both increase by the same amount.
The mean increases much more than the median does.
The median increases much more than the mean does.
Neither the mean nor the median changes.
questions.explanation_md:
- Mean before: $116/5 = 23.2$. After: $196/6 \approx 32.7$, an increase of about 9.5.
- Median before: 23. After: $\frac{23 + 25}{2} = 24$, an increase of 1.

An outlier pulls the mean far more than the median.

distractor_notes.A: The mean rises about 9.5 and the median rises 1.
distractor_notes.C: The reverse is true: the median is resistant to outliers.
distractor_notes.D: Both change; the mean changes a lot.

questions.stem_md: Data set A is $\{10, 20, 30, 40, 50\}$. Data set B is formed by adding 5 to each value in A. Data set C is formed by multiplying each value in A by 2. Which statement is true about the standard deviations of the data sets?
choices: A and B have the same standard deviation, and C’s is larger.
All three data sets have the same standard deviation.
B has the largest standard deviation.
A and C have the same standard deviation, and B’s is larger.
questions.explanation_md: Standard deviation measures spread. Adding the same number to every value shifts the data but doesn’t change the spread, so A and B match. Multiplying every value by 2 doubles all the distances from the mean, so C’s standard deviation is twice A’s.

distractor_notes.B: Scaling by 2 does change the spread.
distractor_notes.C: Shifting doesn’t change the spread at all.
distractor_notes.D: This has the two effects reversed.

questions.stem_md: A scatterplot shows the number of hours students studied, $x$, and their test scores, $y$. The line of best fit is $y = 4.5x + 62$. Based on this model, what is the predicted score for a student who studied 6 hours?

distractor_notes.A: This is the $y$-intercept, the prediction for 0 hours.

questions.stem_md: A study of used cars found that a car’s resale value, $v$ (in thousands of dollars), is modeled by $v = 24 - 1.8a$, where $a$ is the car’s age in years. What is the best interpretation of $1.8$ in this model?
choices: A new car is worth \$1,800.
The predicted value decreases by about \$1,800 for each additional year of age.
Cars lose 1.8% of their value each year.
The average car in the study is 1.8 years old.
questions.explanation_md: 1.8 is the slope: for each additional year ($a$ up by 1), the predicted value changes by $-1.8$ thousand dollars, a decrease of about \$1,800.

distractor_notes.A: A new car ($a = 0$) is predicted to be worth \$24,000.
distractor_notes.C: A linear model loses a fixed amount each year, not a fixed percent.
distractor_notes.D: The slope isn’t an average age.

questions.stem_md:
| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 3 | 6 | 12 | 24 | 48 |

Which type of model best fits the data in the table?
choices: Linear, increasing by 3 each step
Exponential, doubling each step
Linear, increasing by 6 each step
Quadratic, with a minimum at $x = 0$
questions.explanation_md:
The differences are 3, 6, 12, 24, so they aren’t constant and the model isn’t linear. The ratios are $6/3 = 12/6 = 24/12 = 48/24 = 2$, which are constant.

A constant ratio means exponential growth: $y = 3 \cdot 2^x$.

distractor_notes.A: Only the first difference is 3; the differences keep growing.
distractor_notes.D: A quadratic’s *second* differences are constant; here they are 3, 6, 12, which are not.

questions.stem_md: A bag contains 6 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 10 green marbles. If one marble is chosen at random, what is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation_md:
There are $6 + 4 + 10 = 20$ marbles, 4 of them blue.

$$P(\text{blue}) = \frac{4}{20} = \frac{1}{5}$$

distractor_notes.A: This is $\frac{4}{16}$, which divides by the number of non-blue marbles instead of the total.
distractor_notes.C: This is $\frac{4}{10}$, blue compared with green only.
distractor_notes.D: This is $\frac{4}{6}$, blue compared with red only.

questions.stem_md:
| | Owns a pet | Does not own a pet | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lives in an apartment | 18 | 42 | 60 |
| Lives in a house | 51 | 39 | 90 |
| Total | 69 | 81 | 150 |

A survey of 150 people is summarized above. If a person who owns a pet is chosen at random, what is the probability that the person lives in an apartment?
questions.explanation_md:
“If a person who owns a pet is chosen” restricts the group to the 69 pet owners. Of those, 18 live in an apartment.

$$\frac{18}{69} = \frac{6}{23} \approx 0.2608$$

(.2608 or .2609 is also accepted.)

questions.stem_md: A random sample of 400 voters in a city found that 56% support a new library, with a margin of error of 5%. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
choices: Exactly 56% of all voters in the city support the new library.
The percent of all voters in the city who support the library is plausibly between 51% and 61%.
Between 51% and 61% of the voters in the sample support the library.
Fewer than half of the voters in the city support the library.
questions.explanation_md: A margin of error gives a plausible range for the **population** value: $56\% \pm 5\%$, or 51% to 61%.

distractor_notes.A: A sample estimate isn’t exact for the whole population.
distractor_notes.C: The sample value is exactly 56%; the interval describes the population.
distractor_notes.D: The whole plausible range is above 50%.

questions.stem_md: Two researchers estimate the mean height of the same tree species. Researcher A measures a random sample of 50 trees, and Researcher B measures a random sample of 500 trees. Both use the same method. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: Researcher A’s estimate will have a smaller margin of error.
Researcher B’s estimate will have a smaller margin of error.
Both estimates will have the same margin of error.
Researcher B’s estimate will be larger than Researcher A’s.
questions.explanation_md: Larger random samples give more precise estimates, so the margin of error shrinks as the sample size grows. Researcher B’s sample is ten times larger.

distractor_notes.C: The margin of error depends on sample size.
distractor_notes.D: Sample size affects precision, not whether an estimate runs high or low.

questions.stem_md: Researchers surveyed people who visit a gym regularly and found that they reported sleeping better than people who don’t. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Going to the gym causes people to sleep better.
Among the people surveyed, regular gym visits are associated with better reported sleep.
Sleeping better causes people to go to the gym.
Everyone who starts going to the gym will sleep better.
questions.explanation_md: This is an **observational** study: nobody was assigned to go to the gym. It can show an association but not cause and effect, because other factors (such as general health or schedules) could explain both.

distractor_notes.A: Establishing cause and effect requires random assignment to groups.
distractor_notes.C: Causation in either direction isn’t supported.
distractor_notes.D: This overgeneralizes beyond the data, and it’s causal.

questions.stem_md: A school selected 200 students at random from its 1,500 students and randomly assigned half of them to use a new reading app for a semester; the other half did not. The app group’s reading scores improved significantly more. To which group can the result most appropriately be generalized, and what can be concluded?
choices: All students in the country; the app causes improvement.
The 1,500 students at the school; the app likely caused the greater improvement.
Only the 100 students who used the app; no causal conclusion is possible.
The 1,500 students at the school; the app is associated with improvement, but no causal conclusion is possible.
questions.explanation_md:
- **Random selection** from the school’s 1,500 students lets the result generalize to that school.
- **Random assignment** to groups supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.

Both were done, so the app likely caused the improvement for students at that school.

distractor_notes.A: The sample came only from this school, so the result can’t generalize to the whole country.
distractor_notes.C: Random assignment *does* support a causal conclusion, and random selection allows generalizing beyond the sample.
distractor_notes.D: Random assignment allows more than an association.
